description: We are a team focused on programming and technology topics related to space missions. We are interested in creating devices and developing ideas within our technological field.
summary: Echoes in the Dust is an interactive, first-person educational web museum built for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. While students frequently hear about active space missions, iconic spacecraft left behind on the Moon, Mars, asteroids, and deep space often remain buried in dense technical archives. Our web application bridges this gap by giving 13 historic NASA spacecraft—including Apollo 11's Eagle, Lunar Roving Vehicle LRV-1, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Viking 1, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Pioneer 10, and Kepler—a first-person voice tailored for school-age learners and space enthusiasts. Through three-chapter narrative chronicles, voice narration logs, an "Engineering Backpack" linking hardware parts to real scientific discoveries, interactive trivia badges, and live archival imagery fetched directly from NASA's servers, Echoes in the Dust transforms passive reading into engaging STEM discovery.
details:
What It Does & How It Works:

Echoes in the Dust is an interactive, browser-based educational museum requiring zero installation. Users explore 13 real NASA spacecraft resting on the Moon, Mars, asteroids, and deep space by filtering cosmic destinations and opening individual telemetry cards displaying verified coordinates, operational eras, current status, and NSSDCA catalog identifiers.

Key Interactive Features:

1. First-Person 3-Chapter Chronicles: Each spacecraft narrates its mission purpose, scientific breakthroughs, and current state in clear, youth-friendly English.

2. Spacecraft Voice Logs: Integrates the Web Speech API so learners can listen to each chapter narrated aloud.

3. Engineering Backpack: Connects physical hardware components (such as Apollo 11's Laser Ranging Retroreflector, LRV woven piano-wire wheels, Opportunity's spectrometers, and Dawn's xenon ion thrusters) directly to the scientific discoveries they enabled.

4. Live NASA Image Library Feed: Queries NASA's REST API (images-api.nasa.gov) in real time to display authentic archival photography and official NASA IDs inside every mission card.

5. Gamified Trivia & Explorer Certificate: Students unlock mission badges saved locally (localStorage). After unlocking 3 or more badges, an HTML5 Canvas generator creates a downloadable "Junior Space Historian" PNG certificate.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

School-age learners mostly hear about active missions, missing decades of pioneering space history hidden inside dense technical archives. Echoes in the Dust bridges this gap by turning passive reading into active STEM discovery—helping classrooms and casual space fans understand how legacy hardware paved the way for modern exploration.

Creativity & Design Considerations:

Instead of presenting dry encyclopedic timelines, our team gave silent machines an emotional first-person voice combined with a Mission Control HUD aesthetic. Key factors considered included zero-install accessibility across desktop and mobile browsers, 60 FPS rendering performance on low-end hardware, age-appropriate language, and strict scientific accuracy grounded in official NASA catalogs.

Tools, Languages & Software Used:

HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), structured JSON mission datasets, NASA Image and Video Library REST API, Web Speech API, HTML5 Canvas API, Git/GitHub, and GitHub Pages (live at https://axelsin.github.io/echoes-in-the-dust/).
